free fluid collects dependently in the lower abdomen and pelvis; choose a pocket with adequate depth and a short abdominal-wall path.
scan in multiple planes to separate fluid from mobile bowel, liver, spleen, and the urinary bladder.
use color Doppler to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels, collateral veins, and other vessels along the planned tract.
avoid infected skin, surgical scars, abdominal-wall masses, and prominent varices when possible.
fluid and bowel shift when the patient moves; mark immediately before access and keep the patient in the same position.
diagnostic versus therapeutic drainage, requested studies, and the intended volume.
use ultrasound in multiple planes to assess fluid depth, abdominal-wall thickness, and nearby organs.
apply color Doppler and select a site without abdominal-wall vessels.
maintain the mapped position and anesthetize through the abdominal wall to the peritoneum.
use real-time ultrasound for a small or difficult pocket, confirm free return, and advance the catheter without forcing it.
fill the requested specimen tubes first, then drain while monitoring pain, flow, and hemodynamics.
remove the catheter, dress the site, document volume and appearance, and follow the albumin plan for large-volume drainage.
do not attempt a landmark-only puncture when fluid is small, loculated, or obscured by bowel; reposition or use real-time guidance.
avoid abdominal-wall vessels and varices; stop and reassess unexpected bloody return, an enlarging hematoma, hypotension, or increasing pain.
confirm the tract in multiple planes and stop for severe pain, peritoneal signs, or concern for enteric return.
check for catheter kinking, side holes against the wall, loculated fluid, or a shifted pocket before replacing access.
use a small tract, remove the catheter promptly after drainage, and manage ongoing leakage with positioning and an occlusive dressing.
slow or stop drainage for hypotension or symptoms and follow the albumin protocol after large-volume paracentesis.
